title: Lady Poverty
hookLine: Francis marries poverty like a knight marries a lady

lines: A MERCHANT'S SON WHO WANTED GLORY.
KNIGHTS PLEDGE THEMSELVES TO A LADY.
cards: Before he was a saint, Francis wanted to be a knight. His early biographers tell of a cloth merchant's son with fine clothes, generous with his friends, who rode off to war dreaming of glory, and came home changed.
He never quite lost the knight's way of talking. In the old tales of chivalry, a knight pledged his life to a lady and fought in her colors. Francis found a lady too, and she was not a person at all.

teach.b: Francis's biographers say he spoke of poverty as his lady, even as his bride, the one he'd chosen above every other; Saint Bonaventure writes that he called her by those names.
An early allegory goes further, telling of Francis and his brothers climbing a mountain to find Lady Poverty and take her as their companion.

teach.h: A LOVE STORY, NOT A BUDGET.
teach.b: It's a love story, not a budget. Francis's poverty wasn't stinginess or a grim rule. It was courtship.
He went without so his hands would be free for Christ, and for the people Christ loved. Behind it are two lines of Scripture, in the Douay-Rheims.
Jesus tells a rich young man: "If thou wilt be perfect, go sell what thou hast, and give to the poor, and thou shalt have treasure in heaven: and come follow me."
And Paul writes of Christ: "being rich he became poor, for your sakes." Francis wanted to follow the one who became poor. It cost him.
His father, a cloth merchant, brought him before the bishop of Assisi to demand his money back.

Francis gave it back, and then, the story says, took off his clothes, laid them at his father's feet, and said that from now on he would call God his father. The bishop covered him with his own cloak.
Poor for love, not poor for its own sake.
These days have set two ways of giving a life to God side by side: Benedict's houses under one Rule, and Francis on the road.

how: Franciscan friars and Poor Clares make a vow of poverty, owning nothing personally, and Franciscan laypeople try to live simply and share with the poor.

o: a vow to refuse all help from family and friends
going without, for love of Christ who became poor
having too little money to meet your basic needs

p: Francis gave back even his clothes
he became poor, for your sakes

s: for Francis, poverty was a grim rule about money
he spoke of poverty as his lady and bride: going without for love of Christ.
Francis gave his clothes back to his father before the bishop
the story says he laid them at his father's feet and called God his father from then on.
Lady Poverty comes from a modern novel
his early biographers and an early allegory speak of poverty as his lady.

games.q: you're Francis, standing before the bishop of Assisi. your father, a cloth merchant, demands his money back. what do you do?
o: argue that the money was fairly yours.
hand back the money and quietly leave.
give back the money, then take off your clothes and lay them at his feet.
games.why: in the early lives, Francis returns everything, even his clothes, and says he'll call God his father. the bishop covers him with his cloak.

practice: Choose one small thing to go without, the second coffee, the new purchase, the background noise, not as a punishment or to prove anything, but the way Francis did: as making room.
Then ask who that room is for, a person who could use the cost, or the time. If you pray, offer the empty space to God.

wordCard.voice: Poverty. For Francis, not just having less, but a lady he chose: going without for love of Christ, who became poor. Today's word.

orig.note: Latin: Lady Poverty, as Francis's early writers named her.

carryVoice: Your line: poor for love. For Francis it was a courtship, not a grim rule. See you tomorrow.
